questions.question: How do you use hash maps for algorithm patterns in Go?
questions.title: Hash Map Patterns
questions.direct_answer: Two core patterns: (1) Lookup table — build a map of seen values, check for complements (two-sum: seen[target-n]). (2) Counter — count occurrences, group by key. Both convert O(n²) into O(n).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[two-sum: for each n] --> Q{seen[target-n]?}
    Q -->|yes| R[return j, i]
    Q -->|no| S[seen[n] = i]
    S --> A
    C[anagram: for each char] --> INC[counts[r]++]
    INC --> A2[for each char: counts[r]--]
    A2 --> Z[all zero → anagram]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The hash map's complexity contract: average O(1) insert/lookup/delete, worst O(n) (all keys colliding — adversarial input). The average is what algorithmic patterns rely on: the time-space trade is 'O(n) extra memory for O(1) membership.'

The two-sum's invariant, precisely: at iteration i, the map contains exactly the first i-1 elements. Checking seen[target-n] answers 'does the complement exist among elements BEFORE i?' — the answer pair is always (earlier, current), never duplicates. The one-pass solution is the optimized form of the two-pass (build map fully, then check) — same complexity class, half the iterations.

The counter's design vs sorting: isAnagram could sort both strings and compare (O(n log n)) — the counter is O(n). The general principle: when the question is about FREQUENCY or PRESENCE, hashing is O(n); when it's about ORDER, sorting earns its log factor. The interview discipline: identify which question you're answering, choose accordingly.
